title: Housing, with a repayment plan
issue: Borrow now to fund affordable housing and veterans’ housing, or preserve future budget capacity?
no: Reject this bond authorization; existing housing programs are not repealed.
for: US Vets, Habitat for Humanity CA and the CA Federation of Teachers argue that financing can accelerate affordable homes and prevent homelessness.
against: No opposition argument was submitted to the official guide. The substantive tradeoff is debt service and competing budget needs; absence of an argument is not consensus.
cost: Estimated repayments: $500–600 million annually for about 25 years.
check: The campaign’s ‘no new taxes’ language does not mean free. Bond repayments use public resources. Funding homes also does not guarantee any particular reduction in rents.
money: Yes donors include Airbnb ($1m) and OpenAI ($500,000).
interest: Inference: housing providers and construction workers can gain funded projects and jobs; residents can gain homes. A shared benefit does not establish misuse.
values: Housing access and investment today ↔ debt capacity and flexibility tomorrow.

title: A larger rainy-day fund
issue: How much should the state save during good years, and how should those savings interact with spending limits?
yes: Change reserve and debt-payment rules to build larger reserves and extend extra debt payments.
no: Keep current reserve and debt-payment rules.
for: CA Professional Firefighters, the LA Chamber of Commerce and Gavin Newsom support a larger cushion for services during downturns.
against: Assemblymember David Tangipa argues that excluding reserve deposits from the spending limit makes taxpayer rebates less likely.
cost: Higher reserves, with less flexibility to spend or return some money immediately.
check: Saving money does not create new revenue. ‘Protect services’ is a purpose, not a guarantee against cuts; ‘more spending’ does not erase the larger reserve requirement.
money: No donor figures verified for this measure.
interest: Inference: service providers value reliable budgets; taxpayers may value rebates. These are policy stakes, not evidence of personal enrichment.
values: Stability across recessions ↔ present-day spending choices and taxpayer refunds.

title: Keep the high-income tax
issue: Should the existing higher income-tax rates expire or become permanent?
yes: Keep the current high-income tax increase permanently.
no: Let it expire in 2031 under current law.
for: California Teachers Association, California State PTA and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA argue that continuation protects education and health funding.
against: California Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association and California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce argue that a temporary tax should end and spending should improve first.
cost: Maintains an estimated $5–15 billion a year after the scheduled expiration.
check: ‘No tax increase’ compares rates with today. Compared with scheduled law after 2031, affected taxpayers would pay more. A No vote does not end this tax immediately.
money: Yes: CTA Issues PAC contributed about $60.5m.
interest: Inference: education workers and institutions benefit from funding; affected high earners benefit from expiration. Neither interest alone settles the merits.
values: Progressive revenue and public services ↔ honoring sunsets and limiting ongoing tax burdens.

title: Allow public campaign funding
issue: Should governments be allowed to design programs that publicly fund candidates?
yes: Lift the ban, subject to restrictions on eligible funds, candidates and uses.
no: Keep the ban for state and most local governments.
for: League of Women Voters of CA, California Nurses Association and Consumer Watchdog argue public financing can reduce dependence on large donors.
against: California Taxpayers Association and Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association object to using taxes for campaigns and warn about program costs.
cost: A few hundred thousand dollars annually for state advice and administration; future program choices matter.
check: Permission is not a statewide funding program. The measure neither eliminates private political spending nor automatically establishes unlimited payments to candidates.
money: No donor figures verified for this measure.
interest: Inference: qualifying candidates could receive public money; taxpayers fund programs. Claims that every opponent is protecting donor power go beyond that evidence.
values: Broader access to campaigning ↔ opposition to subsidizing political speech with taxes.

title: Separate recall from replacement
issue: Should a recall ballot also choose the replacement?
yes: Remove the replacement question; use succession, appointments or later elections depending on the office.
for: League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause argue that replacements should not win with a small plurality.
against: Brian W. Jones and Joe Patterson argue voters lose their immediate choice of successor and politicians gain appointment power.
cost: Net costs or savings are unknown and depend on the recall and office.
check: This does not abolish recalls. It does remove an immediate electoral choice. Guaranteed savings are not established by the fiscal analysis.
money: No donor figures verified for this measure.
interest: Inference: parties and officeholders face different succession incentives. That is an institutional stake, not proof of a financial payoff.
values: Orderly succession and majority legitimacy ↔ direct, immediate voter choice of replacement.

title: Loans for new-home buyers
issue: Use a bond-funded mortgage program to help eligible middle-income households buy newly built homes?
yes: Create the program with up to $25 billion in revenue bonds repaid by borrowers.
no: Do not require this new assistance program.
for: United Nurses Associations of California, California Conference of Carpenters and Treasurer Fiona Ma argue it expands homeownership without taxpayer repayment.
against: No opposition argument was submitted. Questions remain about eligibility, who can afford the remaining purchase price, and how much assistance translates into more construction.
cost: No direct state or local cost in the official summary; borrowers repay loans.
check: This is a loan, not a free down payment. It targets qualified new homes and eligible buyers, not all renters or existing homes. ‘No taxpayer risk’ is broader rhetoric than ‘no direct cost.’
money: Yes: Realtor-sponsored Homeownership for Families contributed about $18.8m.
interest: Inference: real-estate sales and construction can benefit alongside buyers.
values: Access to ownership and new construction ↔ targeting help toward households with the greatest need.

title: Borrow for immune-system research
issue: Commit long-term public financing to a specific research field and funding structure?
no: Reject these bonds; other medical research funding can continue.
for: Michael J. Fox Foundation, Alzheimer’s Los Angeles and American Nurses Association/CA support research toward treatments and prevention.
against: Researcher Robert M. Kaplan argues the debt and earmarks reduce flexibility and research should compete through the budget process.
cost: $500–600 million annually for roughly 20 years, potentially offset by research revenues.
check: Cures and self-financing are uncertain. ‘Designed’ to avoid taxpayer cost is not a guarantee. Half the bond funding goes to one UC-affiliated nonprofit institute, an important concentration of resources.
interest: Inference: recipient institutions gain funding and influence over research priorities. Philanthropic support is not evidence that a donor personally profits.
values: Public science and long-term discovery ↔ open funding competition and budget flexibility.

title: Add voter identification requirements
issue: Add identification steps to voting, balancing verification and access?
yes: Require government-issued identification in person and identifying numbers on mail-ballot envelopes.
no: Keep signature-based identification under existing rules.
for: The Transparency Foundation and Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association argue identification improves trust in elections.
against: ACLU California Action, Common Cause and League of Women Voters of California argue the rules create unnecessary barriers for eligible voters.
cost: Tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars annually.
check: Popularity does not establish how much fraud a rule prevents. Existing signature verification is not ‘no verification.’ Opponents’ partisan labels do not quantify how many eligible voters would be blocked; that outcome is not established here.
money: Yes: Richard Uihlein $17m. No donors include the California Democratic Party.
interest: Inference: participation rules create political incentives on both sides. The reviewed evidence does not establish a direct commercial payoff.
values: Additional verification and confidence ↔ accessible voting, privacy and administrative cost.

title: A one-time billionaire wealth tax
issue: Raise substantial temporary health funding from wealth while accepting collection and behavioral uncertainty?
yes: Enact a one-time 5% wealth tax on qualifying billionaires.
no: Do not enact this wealth tax.
for: Bernie Sanders and SEIU United Healthcare Workers West argue billionaires should contribute more to health care.
against: California Primary Care Association, California School Boards Association and California Taxpayers Association warn about fiscal and economic consequences.
cost: Tens of billions in temporary revenue; possible ongoing income-tax losses below $1 billion annually, per the analyst.
check: A one-time receipt cannot permanently solve an annual funding gap. Conversely, claims that everyone is directly taxed misdescribe this measure’s billionaire scope. Exact collections and behavioral responses remain uncertain.
money: Yes: SEIU-UHW. No: Building a Better California contributed $158.5m.
interest: Inference: taxed asset owners have a direct financial stake; health workers and providers have a funding stake. Opposition also includes service organizations.
values: Redistribution and health access ↔ predictable taxation, durable revenue and economic uncertainty.

title: Audits—and limits on new taxes
issue: Require audits while restricting new taxes that bypass the state spending limit?
yes: Add pre-ballot and recurring audits, and restrictions on spending-limit exemptions for new taxes.
no: Keep existing audit responsibilities and spending-limit rules.
for: California Society of CPAs, CalAsian Chamber of Commerce and California Taxpayers Association argue audits improve accountability.
against: Bernie Sanders and SEIU-UHW argue the measure is designed to obstruct the billionaire tax.
cost: Net fiscal effect unknown; audits cost money and any resulting savings depend on later decisions.
check: An ‘audits’ description omits a major tax restriction. Audits do not guarantee better outcomes. The potential conflict with Prop. 40 is substantive, but the courts’ eventual interpretation is not certain.
money: Yes: Building a Better California $58.35m. No: SEIU-UHW-backed committee.
interest: Inference: people exposed to new wealth taxation benefit from restrictions; service funders may lose options.
values: Oversight and enforceable spending rules ↔ flexible revenue tools and voters’ ability to fund services.

title: Prohibit new asset-ownership taxes
issue: Constitutionally restrict future personal-property taxation and certain retroactive taxes?
yes: Prohibit new state taxes on owning financial assets and other personal property, with retroactivity limits.
no: Preserve those future taxing options; this vote itself imposes no new tax.
for: CA Professional Firefighters, State Building & Construction Trades Council and AMVETS Department of CA emphasize protecting savings.
against: Bernie Sanders and SEIU-UHW argue the measure protects billionaires from Prop. 40.
cost: Could reduce future revenue relative to what otherwise might be enacted; amount unknown.
check: Protecting savings is broader than the immediate billionaire-tax dispute. The official analysis says simply owning financial assets is not currently taxed; a No vote is not a new retirement-account tax. The ban would extend beyond Prop. 40.
money: Yes: Building a Better California $159.1m. No: SEIU-UHW-backed committee.
interest: Inference: asset owners gain protection from future taxes; government loses an option.
values: Tax predictability and property protection ↔ future flexibility to tax accumulated wealth.

title: A higher bar for local special taxes
issue: Should voter-initiated local special taxes require a majority or two-thirds approval?
yes: Require two-thirds approval for covered taxes beginning January 1, 2027.
no: Keep majority approval for these voter-proposed taxes.
for: California Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association and California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce argue taxes should require broader consent.
against: California Professional Firefighters, California Federation of Teachers and Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA argue the change obstructs funding for essential services.
cost: Future local tax revenues may grow less than under current rules.
check: This does not itself cut existing taxes. A minority can block a tax supported by a majority; whether that is protection or obstruction is the underlying value dispute, not a factual disagreement.
money: Yes: California Business Roundtable PAC $11.64m. No: SEIU committees.
interest: Inference: taxpayers and businesses gain veto protection; publicly funded services and workers face a higher funding hurdle.
values: Majority rule and local services ↔ supermajority consent for new tax burdens.

title: A spending floor for community clinics
issue: Should covered nonprofit clinics have to devote 90% of revenue to program services?
yes: Set the 90% requirement with penalties for covered clinics.
no: Do not impose this new spending requirement.
for: The official pro campaign contact is SEIU-UHW. Supporters argue the rule redirects money toward clinics’ charitable mission and restrains executive spending.
against: American Academy of Pediatrics CA, California Medical Association and California Academy of Family Physicians warn of closures and lost services.
cost: State administration in the low tens of millions annually, covered by fees.
check: Program services include more than direct patient care. A ratio alone does not demonstrate care quality. The claim of hundreds of closures is a campaign prediction, not a verified outcome in the summary.
money: Yes: SEIU-UHW committee. No: AltaMed about $6.13m.
interest: Inference: regulated clinics have a direct operating stake; the union has a workforce stake. Neither establishes that every claimed patient benefit or harm will occur.
values: Spending accountability ↔ operating flexibility and continuity of safety-net care.

title: Faster reviews, narrower challenges
issue: Speed up covered projects by changing environmental review and court procedures?
yes: Apply new deadlines and narrower court-review procedures to eligible projects.
no: Retain existing project-review and court-challenge rules.
for: California Children’s Hospital Association, California Water Association and California Council for Affordable Housing argue faster construction reduces costs.
against: Coalition for Clean Air, CA Environmental Voters and National Wildlife Federation warn about weaker review and public protections.
cost: Initial annual government costs in high tens of millions, possibly over $100 million; longer-term effects uncertain.
check: Faster approval does not guarantee lower household bills. Keeping environmental standards while narrowing enforcement can still change practical protection. Predictions of no affordability benefit are also stronger than the fiscal evidence establishes.
money: Yes: building-industry and utility donors. No: Wendy Schmidt $10m.
interest: Inference: builders and utilities can gain time and lower delay costs; communities bear project impacts. Financial interest does not alone disprove a supply benefit.
values: Housing and infrastructure delivery ↔ environmental enforcement and meaningful public review.
